extracted.intended_audience: British political class and informed public (late 18th-century readers and policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay arguing for preservation of England's established institutions (church, monarchy, aristocracy, and ordered liberties) and warning against revolutionary subversion. It advances moral, religious, legal, and practical standards for judging reforms to the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as the basis of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is the basis of civil society and the source of all good and comfort; it underpins morals, social order, and popular feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The people feel inwardly that religion sustains the state; reforms should not strip away the religious basis because the mind 'will not endure a void' and other harmful superstitions could take its place. Anti-pattern: calling in Atheism or impiety to correct or perfect religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarantine philosophic/atheist cabals
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophic cabals (self-styled 'freethinkers' or atheists) are dangerous and ought to be quarantined from influencing public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such groups are described as an imported, infectious metaphysics; they have no historical standing as a cohesive faction in England and should not be permitted to act as a corporate political force. Example/anti-pattern: allowing a gregarious cabal to actuate public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep an established Church (state religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An established Church is a foundational institution — 'first of our prejudices' — providing consecration of the state and inculcating elevated notions of duty in officeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consecration of the commonwealth by a state religious establishment gives public officers a sense of acting 'in the person of God' and inspires permanence, virtue, and accountability. Anti-pattern: treating church as merely convenient or separable from the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mixed institutions in proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an established church, an established monarchy, an established aristocracy, and an established democracy each 'in the degree it exists, and in no greater.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The balance of these estates forms the English constitution; reforms should not seek to extend any estate beyond its proper degree. Approach faults cautiously rather than by wholesale subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not employ impiety to reform religion
rubrics_metrics.description: If religious tenets need elucidation or ecclesiastical establishment revision, do not call on atheism or impiety to explain or correct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms should be illuminated 'with other lights' and effected through legitimate channels, not by introducing antireligious doctrines into the heart of public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion supplies moral accountability for rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: A religion connected with the state impresses upon those who wield power that they act in trust and are accountable to a higher Master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wholesome awe restrains abuse; without it, magistrates and collective sovereignties risk becoming shameless and fearless. Example: soldiers selling a king for pay illustrates the collapse of moral restraint when accountability fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain popular sovereignty with moral standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The people must be persuaded that their will is not the absolute standard of right and wrong; popular authority unchecked is prone to shamelessness and impunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect democracy is described as 'the most shameless thing in the world'; the public must be taught that liberty does not justify arbitrary use of power. Anti-pattern: equating the people's will with moral correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning reform by subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach state defects with caution; do not begin reformation by subverting the state itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should treat the state as a father with pious awe and trembling solicitude, not hack it to pieces in hopes of regenerating it through radical experiments. Anti-pattern: rashly overthrowing institutions as a method of reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve continuity — the state as intergenerational contract
rubrics_metrics.description: The state is more than a temporary partnership; it is a partnership across generations linking living, dead, and unborn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the ends of the commonwealth span many generations, institutions must maintain continuity; frivolous, fashion-driven alterations break the chain and endanger education, property, and public virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect property rights and legal stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure, certain laws and property-holding are essential for education, industry, arts, and the cultivation of honor and civic virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without stable legal standards and property arrangements, education loses its point, arts and manufactures decline, and successive generations cannot rely on prior achievements; anti-pattern: continual changing of standards and tests of honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve jurisprudence as collective reason of ages
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of jurisprudence, though imperfect, is the collected reason of ages and must be studied and conserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandoning jurisprudence to personal arrogance or transient fashions would eliminate fixed laws that direct actions; reforms should not discard the accumulated legal wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep clergy independent of the Treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: The fixed estate of the Church should not be converted into a pension dependent on the Treasury; clergy must not become ecclesiastical pensioners of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence on the crown or treasury would compromise clergy independence and risk politicizing religion; England made the Church independent to avoid such dangers. Anti-pattern: making clergy financially beholden to political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confiscate Church property
rubrics_metrics.description: Confiscation of church estates is dishonest, perfidious, and cruel; seizure of such property undermines public trust and provokes alarm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass proscription and appropriation of ecclesiastical property is denounced as robbery and sacrilege; example: the National Assembly's confiscations are blamed for rousing public horror and strengthening attachment to Church property elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use church wealth partly for public charity but respect property
rubrics_metrics.description: Some church revenue should be used charitably, but the estate of the Church is identified with private property and should remain stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state is guardian and regulator of church property, not proprietor; it's better to leave much to free will (even with some inefficiency) than to centralize all charitable control. Anti-pattern: treating church wealth as wholly disposable public purse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public ceremonial and visible religion have social value
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious buildings, music, decoration and public solemn acts provide public ornament, consolation, and a sense of dignity for all classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremony elevates the poorest by giving them a sense of importance and links social ranks; visible honors for clergy help affirm national reverence for public virtue. Anti-pattern: relegating religion to obscure or purely private spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical role in education and elite formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastics commonly direct education from infancy to manhood and serve as companions and tutors to young nobility, thereby connecting the elite to the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This educational role liberalizes the Church and helps bind leading characters of the country to ecclesiastical institutions; reforms weakening this role risk severing that formative connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid degrading and wholesale punishment of classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass degradation (driving formerly independent men to live on alms) is an extreme cruelty and greater punishment than death in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscation and social proscription that strip people of independence and fame inflict lasting moral injury; anti-pattern: using confiscation as a fiscal or political expedient.
